note: A lender told a borrower: when you repay me, do it in front of two people who have learned halakha. The borrower repaid him privately, with no one present, and the coins were then taken by forces beyond the lender's control. The lender came before Rav Naḥman: yes, I took the money, but only as a deposit to hold until two learned people came along and the condition could be met, so the loss is not mine. Rav Naḥman said that since he admitted taking it, it was a full repayment. And if he wanted the condition met, let him bring the money now, since Rav Naḥman and Rav Sheshet had learned halakha, Sifra, Sifrei, Tosefta and the whole Talmud.
why: The Gemara is collecting cases about repaying loans before witnesses. Just before, Rava ruled that a lender who names particular witnesses can insist on them; here Rav Naḥman holds that money the lender admits receiving is repaid regardless.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judge who held that the debt had been repaid.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sage named by Rav Naḥman as fully learned, along with himself.

terms.meaning: Early collections of the Sages' teachings, studied alongside the Mishna.
Property held for safekeeping. An unpaid keeper is not liable when it is lost through forces beyond his control.

note: A borrower told his lender: whenever you say I have not repaid, I will believe you as if you were two witnesses. He then repaid the loan in front of three witnesses. Rav Pappa ruled that the lender could not deny it: the borrower had trusted him like two witnesses, not like three. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, objected that following the larger number applies to estimates of value, where more people know more, but in testimony a hundred witnesses are like two and two are like a hundred.
why: The Gemara has just argued over a borrower who makes his lender believable against any claim of repayment, and whether that trust can outweigh witnesses; this case asks whether the number of witnesses changes the answer.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who rules that trust 'like two witnesses' does not stand against three.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who objects that in testimony the number of witnesses beyond two makes no difference.

terms.meaning: The rule that when people disagree, the view held by more of them is accepted. Rav Huna says it fits estimates of value, not testimony.
